I am a manager in financial services with a strong quantitative and technical background, currently based in the Zurich office of a European consulting boutique. I consult on risk, insurance and asset management topics where analytical modelling, regulatory expertise and software engineering intersect. My work focuses on translating regulatory and business requirements into practical, data-driven solutions that strengthen risk frameworks and investment processes.
I hold an MBA from Mannheim Business School and a PhD in Statistical Physics focused on nonequilibrium thermodynamics and Monte Carlo simulations, completed under the supervision of Prof. M. Esposito. I also hold an MSc with distinction in Theoretical Physics. Further, being a CFA Charterholder and active member of CFA Society Switzerland, complements my quantitative background with expertise in investment analysis, portfolio management and professional ethics.
# About # This website is a compact map of my work across financial services consulting, quantitative risk, asset management and technical implementation. The project section highlight selected client work at the boundary between regulation, models, data and software; the academic sections collect publications and talks from my research in statistical physics; and the blog is where I connect practical delivery experience with broader questions in risk management, investment processes and technology.
You can explore the main areas here:

Introduction and MotivationWe recently published a whitepaper on the Solvency II Review, focusing on the new Long-Term Guarantees (LTG) measures — in particular interest-rate extrapolation and the volatility adjustment.
The paper provides a detailed analysis of both methodologies and the practical challenges observed during implementation.
Extrapolation: Introducing Market SensitivityThe current Smith-Wilson approach enforces a direct convergence to the Ultimate Forward Rate (UFR), largely ignoring market information beyond the Last Liquid Point.
The revised method introduces the Last Liquid Forward Rate (LLFR) as an intermediate step. By blending market forward rates with the UFR, the extrapolated curve becomes sensitive to long-term market conditions.
Quantitatively, this changes the mechanics:
If LLFR > UFR → higher discount rates → increase in own fundsIf LLFR < UFR → lower discount rates → decrease in own fundsThe direction of impact is therefore no longer fixed, but depends on the market environment.
Volatility Adjustment: From Uniform to SpecificThe revised volatility adjustment introduces a key new component: the Credit Spread Sensitivity Ratio (CSSR), which links the adjustment to the relative spread sensitivities of assets and liabilities.
CSSR ≈ PVBP(Assets) / PVBP(Liabilities)This makes the VA:
undertaking-specificdependent on balance sheet structureWhile the increase in the application ratio raises baseline VA levels, the CSSR acts as a dampening factor. The net effect varies across undertakings and scenarios.
Implementation & TakeawaysWhile the conceptual changes to the LTG framework are well-motivated, the real challenge lies in implementation. Both extrapolation and the revised volatility adjustment introduce additional dependencies on market data, sensitivities, and undertaking-specific characteristics — turning what used to be relatively stable adjustments into dynamic components of the valuation framework.
In practice, several challenges consistently emerge:
CSSR computation: The ratio requires consistent spread sensitivity measures for both assets and liabilities. Depending on the setup, these must be derived either in risk systems or cash-flow models — often with different approximations.Scenario dependency: In stochastic models, sensitivities are not constant. Especially in tail scenarios, shifts in spreads and interest rates can materially change the CSSR, introducing additional variability in own funds.Closing constraints: The CSSR must be available early in the reporting process, despite its computational complexity. This often leads to approximations or pre-calculation strategies.Group-level consistency: Different undertakings may exhibit materially different CSSR levels, implying different VA levels across entities and increasing the complexity of group modelling.From a quantitative perspective, the combined effect of the LTG changes is a shift in how valuation reacts to inputs:
Extrapolation becomes sensitive to long-term market structure via the LLFRThe VA becomes a function of balance sheet sensitivities via the CSSROwn funds become more dependent on both market conditions and internal modelling choicesThis increases realism — but also reduces predictability. In particular, results can vary more strongly across scenarios and undertakings, even under similar market conditions.
In short: the Solvency II Review moves the framework towards greater market consistency and risk sensitivity, but at the cost of higher model complexity, increased operational burden, and a stronger dependence on modelling assumptions.

title: Solvency II Review: Rethinking Long-Term Guarantees

content:
How It BeganMy journey with the Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) Program began out of curiosity rather than ambition. I wanted to understand financial systems more deeply, and the CFA curriculum appeared to offer a structured path. At the time, I had little idea of the scope, discipline, and time that the program would require. What started as an interest in learning soon became a multi-year process of structured study and reflection.
The CurriculumThe program is divided into three levels, each with its own focus and character. I found the structure of the curriculum exceptionally well designed. It combines technical precision with a broad understanding of markets and human behavior.
Level I introduces the foundations. It covers quantitative methods, economics, financial reporting and analysis, corporate finance, and ethics. It creates a strong technical base and establishes the professional standards that define the CFA designation.Level II moves from theory to application. It concentrates on valuation techniques, equity and fixed income analysis, derivatives, and portfolio management concepts. The analytical depth at this stage is considerable, and it develops the discipline to approach problems methodically.Level III focuses on integration. It applies previous knowledge to real-world portfolio management and wealth planning scenarios. It also introduces behavioral finance, which adds an important human dimension to financial decision-making.I appreciated how the curriculum combined quantitative rigor with conceptual understanding. It is comprehensive without being redundant, and it builds a logical progression from technical detail to professional judgment.
Preparation, Results, and ReflectionsThe CFA Program required steady effort over several years. I studied alongside professional responsibilities and maintained a consistent routine. The emphasis was on persistence rather than intensity, and structured preparation proved decisive. I passed all three levels on the first attempt.
The program strengthened both technical knowledge and professional judgment. It trained precision, patience, and respect for detail, while also reinforcing the importance of ethics and consistency. More than a test of endurance, it offered a comprehensive framework for understanding financial markets and decision-making under complexity. Completing the program was not an endpoint but a foundation. It continues to shape how I think about risk, value, and responsibility in finance. The experience confirmed that depth and discipline remain the most valuable long-term investments.
Following completion, I joined CFA Society Switzerland. I look forward to engaging with professionals who share a commitment to continuous learning and high standards in the financial industry. It is an opportunity to exchange ideas, stay connected to current developments, and continue personal and professional growth.
More information about the CFA Institute and the CFA Program can be found on the CFA Institute website.Image courtesy of the CFA Institute. All rights reserved.

The ChallengeExport Credit Agencies (ECAs) insure risks that commercial insurers avoid: long-term, high-risk, and often politically uncertain transactions. While pricing export credit insurance policies is already complex, pricing modifications to these policies is an even greater challenge. There are no regulatory guidelines, no established market benchmarks, and each export case exhibits unique characteristics and therefore idiosyncratic risk profiles.
A Unified Mathematical FrameworkColleagues from Schweizerische Exportrisikoversicherung (SERV) and I tackled this challenge in a whitepaper:
Our whitepaper introduces a mathematical framework that brings structure to this problem. It starts by examining existing models for the initial pricing of export credit insurances and then introduces a central quantity: the Specific Risk Premium. As shown, this quantity allows for a standardized pricing across different export credit insurance modifications by aligning the idiosyncratic risks with the corresponding protection offered by the ECA. The result? A pricing methodology that enables ECAs to apply a unified approach across a diverse range of export business cases — ensuring fairness, efficiency, and better risk management.
Why This MattersIn an industry where no two transactions are alike, a structured approach to pricing modifications is essential. Whether extending repayment terms, increasing coverage, or adjusting policy terms post-inception, the ability to price these changes fairly is crucial for ECAs, banks, and exporters.
Curious? Dive into the full whitepaper here and explore how this framework helps bring order to the challenge of pricing export credit insurance modifications.

From left to right: Heribert Knittlmayer (SERV), Aurelio Caliaro (SERV) and me.

The MBA JourneyEmbarking on the two-year Mannheim Business School MBA journey has been a truly transformative experience — both personally and professionally. What stood out most was the uniquely diverse and international environment, where classmates from varied professional, cultural, and personal backgrounds came together. This diversity enriched every discussion and constantly challenged my perspectives.
A defining aspect of the program was the team-driven nature of nearly every assignment. With teams rotating frequently, each new project brought fresh dynamics and personalities, requiring quick adaptation to different working styles and expectations. Interestingly, I often found myself in leadership roles, carrying the added pressure of steering these diverse teams effectively toward our goals. Balancing personalities, identifying individual strengths, and ensuring cohesion under tight deadlines became a recurring challenge — one that pushed me far beyond my comfort zone and honed my interpersonal skills.
The Business Master ProjectThe Business Master Project is widely regarded as the cornerstone of the Mannheim MBA — an opportunity to apply everything learned throughout the program to a real-world business challenge. Over the course of nearly a year, our team had the privilege of collaborating closely with IONITY, our sponsoring company, on a highly engaging and forward-looking project.
Our research focused on exploring the business potential of leveraging electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure for digital out-of-home (DOOH) advertising. Specifically, we evaluated strategic business models and assessed their profitability using net present value as the decision metric. Due to confidentiality agreements, the detailed analytical approach and results cannot be shared here.
Throughout this project, I took on the leadership role — splitting the project into modules, defining deliverables and timelines, keeping the team aligned on our objectives, and driving progress. At times, driving progress meant pushing the team (hopefully not too hard) and reallocating tasks to ensure we stayed on track and met the high standards we set for ourselves. While this project certainly felt stressful at times, I hope the team shares my confidence in the quality of our work, which was also recognized by the academic panel during the evaluation of our final thesis defense.
Looking back, this project stands out as a highlight of the MBA — a powerful blend of academic challenge and people management that left a lasting impact on my personal and professional development.

content:
Six Decades of Capital Market ResearchThe question of what constitutes an optimal investment portfolio has been at the heart of capital market research for decades. Traditionally, the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), developed by William Sharpe and based on Harry Markowitz’s Modern Portfolio Theory, posits that the market portfolio—a fully diversified basket of all investable assets—represents the most efficient investment. According to CAPM, expected returns depend solely on systematic market risk (beta), meaning individual investors cannot achieve excess returns through stock selection or market timing. However, empirical studies have repeatedly challenged this assumption, leading to the emergence of factor investing.
Factor investing builds upon CAPM by identifying additional risk premia beyond market beta. The pioneering work of Eugene Fama and Kenneth French introduced the three-factor model, which incorporates not just market risk but also size (small-cap stocks outperforming large caps) and value (stocks with high book-to-market ratios generating excess returns). Later, Mark Carhart extended this to a four-factor model by including momentum—the tendency of stocks that have performed well in the past to continue outperforming. Further refinements introduced the quality factor (Robert Novy-Marx), which rewards companies with strong profitability metrics, and even broader multi-factor models aiming to capture persistent return drivers.
The ProblemWhile factor investing has historically been supported by empirical data, recent years have seen a significant underperformance of key factor portfolios—particularly value stocks—compared to simple market-cap-weighted index funds. This has led to renewed debates about the long-term persistence of factor premia and whether these excess returns were merely historical artifacts rather than robust market inefficiencies. The so-called post-publication effect suggests that once a factor is widely recognized and exploited, its return premium may disappear due to arbitrage and increased investor participation.
Analysis and ConclusionsIn light of these debates, the question arises: should a retail investor still follow the market-neutral approach of CAPM or can factor-based strategies indeed offer superior risk-adjusted returns? To shed light on this pressing question, the historical market data and the performance of factor investing strategies under different economic environments as well as the real-world constraints of factor investing and its implications on portfolio implementation are examined in the following paper:
The central conclusion of the paper is that, while the empirical evidence does not conclusively rule out the continued existence of certain factor premia, their practical exploitability for retail investors is severely constrained. Transaction costs, turnover, tax inefficiencies, model instability, and regulatory frictions significantly erode the theoretical excess returns suggested by academic models. In particular, once factors are widely disseminated and incorporated into investable products, their performance tends to weaken, consistent with the post-publication effect observed in the literature. As a result, the paper argues that a broadly diversified, market-cap-weighted buy-and-hold portfolio—designed to be cost-efficient, tax-efficient, and robust across market regimes—remains the most reliable and economically sound investment strategy for retail investors.
